passages.t: Five thousand fed, and a crown refused
passages.happening:
Jesus crosses to the far side of the Sea of Galilee. A large crowd follows him, because they have seen him heal the sick. It is near Passover (verse 4).

Jesus sees the crowd coming and asks Philip, “Where can we buy bread for these people to eat?” (verse 5). John tells us Jesus already knew what he would do; he was testing Philip. Philip does the sums: “Two hundred denarii would not buy enough bread for each of them to have a small piece” (verse 7). Andrew finds a boy “with five barley loaves and two small fish. But what difference will these make among so many?” (verse 9).

Jesus has the people sit down on the grass, about five thousand men. He takes the loaves, gives thanks, and hands them out, and the fish too, as much as anyone wants. When all are full, he tells the disciples to gather the pieces “so that nothing will be wasted” (verse 12). They fill twelve baskets.

The people say, “Truly this is the Prophet who is to come into the world” (verse 14). And Jesus, seeing that they are about to seize him and make him king by force, slips away to the mountain alone (verse 15).
passages.hearers:
This is one of the few events told in all four Gospels. The notes on Mark 6:30-44 and Matthew 14:13-21 explain the denarius (a day's wage), the wilderness and the twelve baskets. John adds details of his own.

Barley loaves. Wheat bread was the better bread; barley was cheaper, and barley bread was what poorer people ate. The boy's lunch was a poor family's food: a few small loaves and two small fish to eat with them.

Passover. John alone says the feast was near. Passover remembered God bringing Israel out of Egypt, and the years of manna in the wilderness that followed. A crowd fed with bread in a lonely place at Passover time would think of Moses.

That is why they say ‘the Prophet’. They mean the prophet like Moses whom God had promised. And their next thought is a king. Many hoped for a leader who would drive out Rome. A man who could feed an army in the wilderness looked like that leader. Jesus will not be that kind of king. He walks away from the crown they offer. The crown he will be given in this Gospel is made of thorns (19:2).
passages.ot: Two stories stand behind this one. In the wilderness God said to Moses, “Behold, I will rain down bread from heaven for you” (Exodus 16:4). And the prophet Elisha once fed a hundred men with “twenty loaves of barley bread”; his servant asked how that could be enough, and the LORD said, “They will eat and have some left over” (2 Kings 4:42-43). Barley loaves, a doubting helper, and food left over: John's hearers would catch the echo. Jesus does what Elisha did, on a far larger scale, and what God did for Israel in the desert.
passages.hard:
Did this really happen? Some modern readers have said the crowd had food hidden away and shared it when they saw the boy's example. John gives no hint of that. The crowd's own response, trying to make Jesus king, shows they thought they had seen a wonder. The note on Matthew 14 sets out this question more fully: in the end, how a reader weighs this story turns on whether God acts in the world at all.

And why does Jesus refuse to be king, if he is the Messiah? Because the crowd wanted the wrong kind of king, a ruler who would fill stomachs and fight Rome. Jesus is a king, as he will tell Pilate, but “My kingdom is not of this world” (18:36).
passages.asks:
The boy gave what he had, and it was not much. Andrew thought it was too small to matter. Jesus took it and gave thanks for it. If what you have to offer looks pitiful next to the need, that is no reason to hold it back.

And notice that the crowd loved Jesus for what he could give them and tried to make him serve their plans. It is possible to want Jesus very much and still want him on our own terms.

passages.t: It is I; do not be afraid
passages.happening:
That evening the disciples set off by boat across the lake toward Capernaum. It is dark, and Jesus has not come. A strong wind is blowing and the sea is rough.

They have rowed about three or four miles when they see Jesus walking on the sea, coming near the boat. They are terrified. He says to them, “It is I; do not be afraid” (verse 20). They want to take him into the boat, and at once the boat reaches the shore they were heading for.
passages.hearers:
Mark and Matthew tell this story too (Mark 6:45-52; Matthew 14:22-33), and their notes say more. John tells it in only six verses, with no calming of the wind and no Peter on the water.

‘Three or four miles’ is in Greek ‘twenty-five or thirty stadia’; a stadion was a Greek measure of a little under two hundred metres. They are far out on the water, in the middle of the lake, in the dark.

The words ‘It is I’ are, in Greek, egō eimi, ‘I am’. In ordinary speech they mean ‘It's me’. But they are also the words the Greek Old Testament uses when God names himself. Scholars debate how much of that a reader should hear here. John will use ‘I am’ many times, beginning in this very chapter with ‘I am the bread of life’ (verse 35).
passages.ot: In the Old Testament only God walks on the sea. Job says God “treads on the waves of the sea” (Job 9:8). A psalm says to God, “Your path led through the sea, Your way through the mighty waters” (Psalm 77:19). And another psalm tells of sailors in a storm whom God brought safely in: “He guided them to the harbor they desired” (Psalm 107:30). The disciples reach the shore at once.
passages.asks: Jesus came to the disciples when it was dark, the wind was against them, and he seemed to be absent. The first words he spoke were not a rebuke but a comfort: it is I; do not be afraid. If you are rowing hard in the dark tonight, those words are for you too.

passages.happening:
The next day the crowd looks for Jesus. They know he did not get into the boat with the disciples. When they find him in Capernaum they ask, “Rabbi, when did You get here?” (verse 25).

Jesus does not answer the question. He tells them why they are really looking for him: not because they saw signs, but because they ate the loaves and were full. “Do not work for food that perishes, but for food that endures to eternal life, which the Son of Man will give you” (verse 27).

They ask what works God wants. Jesus answers, “The work of God is this: to believe in the One He has sent” (verse 29). They ask for a sign. Moses gave our fathers manna, they say, “as it is written: ‘He gave them bread from heaven to eat’” (verse 31). Jesus answers that it was not Moses who gave the bread from heaven, but his Father, who now gives “the true bread from heaven” (verse 32). “Sir,” they say, “give us this bread at all times” (verse 34).
passages.hearers:
Notice how much the crowd's answer sounds like the Samaritan woman's in chapter 4: ‘Sir, give me this water’. Both take Jesus' words about lasting food and water as if he meant the ordinary kind. John tells many of his stories this way. People hear the lower meaning; Jesus means the higher one.

Their request for a sign is odd, since they ate the loaves only yesterday. But they are setting a standard. Moses gave bread every day for forty years. One meal on a hillside looks small beside that. If Jesus is the prophet like Moses, they want to see daily bread from heaven again.

‘The work of God’ in verse 29 is a play on words. They ask what works they must do. Jesus says there is one work, and it is God's work in them: believing in the one God sent.
passages.ot: The crowd quotes Scripture: “He gave them bread from heaven to eat”. Their words echo a psalm, “He rained down manna for them to eat; He gave them grain from heaven” (Psalm 78:24), and the Exodus story itself (Exodus 16:4, 15). Moses had already taught that the manna pointed beyond itself: God fed Israel “so that you might understand that man does not live on bread alone, but on every word that comes from the mouth of the LORD” (Deuteronomy 8:3). Isaiah asked, “Why spend money on that which is not bread, and your labor on that which does not satisfy?” (Isaiah 55:2).
passages.asks: Jesus says the crowd followed him for the loaves. Many people come to God for what he gives: health, success, a calmer life. He does not turn them away. But he will not let them stop there. He asks us to want him, and not only his gifts.

passages.t: I am the bread of life
passages.happening:
Now Jesus says it plainly. “I am the bread of life. Whoever comes to Me will never hunger, and whoever believes in Me will never thirst” (verse 35). The bread from heaven is not a thing he gives. It is himself.

But, he says, you have seen me and still do not believe. Then he speaks of the Father's will. “Everyone the Father gives Me will come to Me, and the one who comes to Me I will never drive away” (verse 37). He came down from heaven to do the Father's will, and the Father's will is that he lose none of those the Father has given him, but raise them up at the last day. “For it is My Father's will that everyone who looks to the Son and believes in Him shall have eternal life, and I will raise him up at the last day” (verse 40).
passages.hearers:
‘I am the bread of life’ is the first of seven sayings in John where Jesus says ‘I am’ and then names a picture: bread, light, door, shepherd, resurrection, way, vine. Each one takes something people need to live and says: that is what I am.

Bread was the centre of every meal in that world. To say ‘I am bread’ was to say ‘you cannot live without me’.

Verse 37 has two halves, and each matters. ‘Everyone the Father gives Me will come to Me’: the coming starts with God. ‘The one who comes to Me I will never drive away’: no one who comes will be turned back. The Greek is very strong, a double ‘no’: he will by no means throw out anyone who comes.
passages.ot: The promise of never hungering and never thirsting is the prophets' promise. Isaiah called, “Come, all you who are thirsty, come to the waters” (Isaiah 55:1), and in the same chapter God says that his word “will not return to Me empty” (Isaiah 55:11). Jesus is that word, come down like rain from heaven.
passages.hard:
Verse 37 and the verses after it raise the question of God's choosing. That question comes back sharply in verse 44, and the note on verses 41-51 sets out how Christians have read it.

Here it is enough to see what verse 37 does not say. It does not say anyone who wants to come will be refused. It says the opposite. Whatever else Christians believe about God's choosing, every tradition agrees on this line: whoever comes to Jesus will never be driven away.
passages.asks: If you fear that you are not one of the people God wants, read verse 37 slowly. Jesus does not say ‘I will check whether you were chosen’. He says ‘the one who comes to Me I will never drive away’. Many Christians believe that the wish to come is itself a sign that God is already drawing you. Come.

passages.t: No one can come unless the Father draws him
passages.happening:
Now ‘the Jews’ begin to grumble because he said, “I am the bread that came down from heaven” (verse 41). They say, “Is this not Jesus, the son of Joseph, whose father and mother we know?” (verse 42).

Jesus says, “Stop grumbling among yourselves” (verse 43). Then: “No one can come to Me unless the Father who sent Me draws him, and I will raise him up at the last day” (verse 44). The prophets wrote that all will be taught by God, and everyone who has heard the Father and learned from him comes to Jesus.

He says it again: “I am the bread of life” (verse 48). Your fathers ate manna in the wilderness, and they died. This bread comes down from heaven so that anyone may eat and not die. “I am the living bread that came down from heaven. If anyone eats of this bread, he will live forever. And this bread, which I will give for the life of the world, is My flesh” (verse 51).
passages.hearers:
‘The Jews’ here are not the Jerusalem leaders of chapter 5. This is a synagogue in Capernaum, in Galilee (verse 59). The phrase seems to mean the Jewish listeners in that synagogue, Galileans who knew Jesus' family. Every person in the scene is Jewish, Jesus included, and in verse 60 his own disciples make the same complaint. John's book page explains the different ways John uses the phrase, and why it must never be turned against the Jewish people.

Their objection is natural. We know his parents. How can a local man say he came down from heaven? People who have known you since childhood find it hardest to see anything great in you.

‘Grumble’ is the word for Israel in the wilderness, complaining against Moses about the food. John's hearers would catch it.

The last line of verse 51 turns a corner. The bread is ‘My flesh’, given ‘for the life of the world’. For the first time in the chapter Jesus speaks of giving himself up, of his death. The bread will be his own body, given.
passages.ot: The grumbling echoes the desert: “there in the desert they all grumbled against Moses and Aaron” (Exodus 16:2). And ‘they will all be taught by God’ (verse 45) comes from Isaiah: “Then all your sons will be taught by the LORD” (Isaiah 54:13). Isaiah was speaking of the day when God would restore his people. Jesus says that day is here, and those who are taught by God come to him.
passages.hard:
What does ‘No one can come to Me unless the Father who sent Me draws him’ mean? Does God draw some and not others? And if so, are those who do not come to blame?

Christians have read these verses in different ways for centuries, and these notes do not choose between them. Those who stress God's choosing say that coming to Christ is always God's free gift. Read with verse 37, verse 44 says that all whom the Father gives will come, and that no one comes without being drawn. On this view the drawing always reaches its goal, and people who refuse are still responsible, because they refuse what they do not want (verse 36). Those who stress human response point to 12:32, where Jesus uses the same Greek verb: “And I, when I am lifted up from the earth, will draw everyone to Myself.” On this view God draws all people by his grace, and each person is truly free to answer or to turn away. Catholic and Orthodox teachers, each in their own way, hold that God's grace always comes first and that the human answer to it is still free.

Both sides agree on a great deal. Salvation begins with God, not with us. No one can boast of finding God by being clever. Those who refuse are responsible for refusing (verse 36). And no one who comes is turned away (verse 37). These notes leave the deeper question where faithful Christians have left it, open for discussion and not a cause for division.

What these verses must never be used for is to tell anyone they cannot come. The same Jesus who said verse 44 said verse 37.
passages.asks: The people in the synagogue could not get past what they already knew about Jesus: Joseph's son, from a family they knew. Sometimes what keeps us from Jesus is not ignorance but familiarity. We think we know him already. Ask whether you have let him be more than you expected.

passages.t: Eat My flesh and drink My blood
passages.happening:
The listeners begin to argue: “How can this man give us His flesh to eat?” (verse 52).

Jesus does not soften it. He makes it stronger. “Truly, truly, I tell you, unless you eat the flesh and drink the blood of the Son of Man, you have no life in you” (verse 53). “Whoever eats My flesh and drinks My blood has eternal life, and I will raise him up at the last day. For My flesh is real food, and My blood is real drink” (verses 54-55). Whoever eats his flesh and drinks his blood “remains in Me, and I in him” (verse 56).

Just as the Father sent him and he lives because of the Father, so the one who feeds on him will live because of him. Unlike the fathers who ate manna and died, whoever eats this bread will live forever. John adds that Jesus said this while teaching in the synagogue at Capernaum (verse 59).
passages.hearers:
These words would shock a Jewish hearer. The Law of Moses forbade drinking blood, even an animal's, because the life is in the blood. Eating human flesh belonged to the worst horrors the Bible could describe. Jesus knew all this, and he said it anyway.

Look at the verb, too. Up to verse 53 John uses the ordinary Greek word for ‘eat’. From verse 54 he switches to a blunter word, trōgō, used of chewing or munching. Jesus is not backing away from the hard saying. He is pressing it.

John's first readers already shared the Lord's Supper, eating bread and drinking from a cup as Jesus told them. When they heard ‘eat My flesh and drink My blood’ they could hardly help thinking of that table. And John alone, of the four Gospels, tells no words over the bread and cup at the Last Supper. Some think this chapter is where he says what the others say there.
passages.ot: The Law said, “For the life of the flesh is in the blood” (Leviticus 17:11), and long before, God told Noah, “you must not eat meat with its lifeblood still in it” (Genesis 9:4). The same verse in Leviticus goes on: “it is the blood that makes atonement for the soul”. So blood meant life, given up to God. When Jesus says that his blood is real drink and gives life, he is speaking of his own life poured out, which the Law's sacrifices had pointed toward.
passages.hard:
Is Jesus speaking here of the Lord's Supper, of believing in him, or of both? Christians have read these verses differently, and the disagreement is old and serious. Each church's view is given here as its own teachers state it.

The Catholic and Orthodox churches read these verses as Jesus' teaching on the Eucharist, the Lord's Supper, in which they believe the bread and wine truly become his body and blood. The Catechism of the Catholic Church calls this chapter ‘the first announcement of the Eucharist’ (paragraph 1336).

Lutherans teach that Christ's body and blood are truly present in, with, and under the bread and wine; they rest that teaching on Jesus' words at the Last Supper, ‘This is My body’. Many Lutheran teachers read John 6 itself as being mainly about faith, not the Supper, and some Lutheran scholars see the Supper here as well.

Many Reformed churches teach that Christ is truly present by his Spirit and that believers feed on him by faith. John Calvin, in his commentary on John, said that this passage is not directly about the Supper but about the feeding on Christ that believers have all the time by faith. He added that what it describes is pictured and truly given to believers in the Supper.

Many Baptist and other churches read these verses as a vivid way of speaking about believing in Jesus and receiving his death for us. They point to verse 35, where coming and believing end hunger and thirst, and to verse 47, “he who believes has eternal life”. When the reformers argued about the Supper at Marburg in 1529, the Swiss side pressed verse 63: “The Spirit gives life; the flesh profits nothing.”

These notes do not settle the question. Every one of these churches agrees that Jesus here offers himself, given in death, as the only true life, and that this life is received, not earned.
passages.asks: Whatever your church teaches about the Lord's Supper, this passage asks something deeper than a view. Jesus does not offer advice to follow or an example to copy. He offers himself, as food. You cannot live on someone else's meal. Each person must come and receive him.

passages.happening:
Many of his disciples hear this and say, “This is a difficult teaching. Who can accept it?” (verse 60). Jesus knows they are grumbling. “Does this offend you?” he asks. What if you see the Son of Man going up to where he was before? “The Spirit gives life; the flesh profits nothing. The words I have spoken to you are spirit and they are life” (verse 63). Some of them do not believe, he says, and that is why he told them no one can come unless the Father grants it.

“From that time on many of His disciples turned back and no longer walked with Him” (verse 66).

Jesus turns to the Twelve. “Do you want to leave too?” (verse 67). Simon Peter answers, “Lord, to whom would we go? You have the words of eternal life. We believe and know that You are the Holy One of God” (verses 68-69).

Jesus answers that he chose all twelve, “Yet one of you is a devil!” (verse 70). John explains: he meant Judas, son of Simon Iscariot, one of the Twelve, who would betray him.
passages.hearers:
The crowd that wanted to crown Jesus on the hillside is gone. Now many of his own followers walk away. What began with five thousand fed on a hillside ends with a handful left.

Verse 63 has been read in more than one way. Some take ‘the flesh profits nothing’ to mean that Jesus' talk of eating his flesh must be understood spiritually, not as eating meat. Others say ‘the flesh’ here means human nature on its own, which cannot understand God without the Spirit, so that it does not cancel what he has just said. The note on verses 52-59 sets out how churches read the whole passage.

Peter's answer is not a confident one. He does not say ‘we understand’. He says, in effect, ‘we have nowhere else to go’. And then he says what he does know: you have the words of eternal life, and you are the Holy One of God.

Jesus' words about Judas are startling. A devil, among the Twelve. Elsewhere Jesus calls Peter ‘Satan’ when Peter tries to turn him from the cross (Mark 8:33). In both places the word names someone doing the enemy's work, not a creature who is not human. John says later that Satan entered Judas (13:27).
passages.ot: Turning back from God is an old story in the Scriptures. The same desert that gave Israel manna saw the people grumble and want to go back to Egypt. And the prophets often found that only a few remained faithful. Isaiah spoke of God's word going out and not returning empty (Isaiah 55:11). The word does its work, even when many walk away.
passages.hard:
If Jesus chose Judas, knowing he would betray him, why did he choose him? John says Jesus knew ‘from the beginning’ who would betray him (verse 64). John does not explain why Jesus chose him anyway. Christians have said different things: that Judas was truly given a place and truly threw it away; that God works even through betrayal to bring about the cross; that the choosing here is to be one of the Twelve, not to be saved. The text does not settle Judas's end, and these notes do not either.

And what about people who turn back? Verse 66 does not hide it, and verse 65 links it to God's granting. Read with verse 37, this is not a door slammed on anyone who wants to come. The same Jesus who saw many leave turned to the Twelve with a question, not a threat: ‘Do you want to leave too?’ He let them choose.
passages.asks:
Many readers live where these disciples stood. Your doubts are real. Some of Jesus' words are hard, and you are not sure you can accept them. People you respect have walked away. Peter did not have every answer either. He stayed because he could find no one else who had the words of eternal life. Staying with honest questions is a kind of faith.

If someone you love has turned away from Jesus, notice that he did not chase the departing crowd with threats, and he did not force the Twelve to stay. He asked them. You can keep praying for the one who left, and leave room for them to come back.
